The Pakistan the world keeps missing. [ dawn ]
item.description:
International standards are often assumed to be a modern invention. They are not. Many predate the United Nations itself; the International Labour Organization (ILO), for instance, was established under the League of Nations and only later folded into the UN system. Countries have long used such standards to strengthen governance, build credibility, and integrate into the global economy.

Pakistan has been one of them.

Over the decades, it has voluntarily become a party to numerous international treaties and conventions, incorporating many of their provisions into its Constitution, national legislation, and regulatory framework, including constitutional guarantees relating to fundamental rights, labour protections and environmental governance.

It is, however, worth remembering that joining an international treaty is a sovereign, voluntary decision. Pakistan took on these obligations because they were seen as consistent with its long-term development goals, not because it was compelled to.

Today, the country is party to well over 150 major international treaties, conventions, and protocols spanning governance, trade, labour, human rights, environmental protection, maritime affairs, and more.

Far from being symbolic, these commitments strengthen market access, attract international investment, support development cooperation and trade negotiations, and reassure global buyers about the credibility of Pakistan’s regulatory framework. Many of them, notably, were undertaken decades before concepts like ESG, carbon border measures, and supply-chain due diligence became central to global trade.

The labour record: ahead of the pack

Pakistan’s commitment to international labour standards illustrates this long-standing pattern well. The country has ratified 38 ILO conventions and one protocol, including eight of the 10 Fundamental Conventions — covering the abolition of forced labour, minimum working age, freedom of association, collective bargaining, equal remuneration, non-discrimination, and the elimination of child labour.

The remaining two — Convention No. 155 on Occupational Safety and Health and Convention No. 187 on the Promotional Framework for Occupational Safety and Health — are currently under active consideration for ratification. Pakistan has also ratified two of the four ILO Governance (Priority) Conventions, on labour inspection and tripartite consultation.

Why does this matter? Because labour standards increasingly determine market access, particularly for export-oriented economies in Asia.

Pakistan has also ratified the Protocol of 2014 to the Forced Labour Convention, signalling its commitment to global best practices and reassuring international buyers that its exports meet internationally recognised labour standards. Tellingly, India has not yet ratified this protocol, despite its labour-related commitments under its free trade agreement with the European Union. Several major Asian textile and apparel exporters — including China, Vietnam, and Cambodia — have not ratified it either, despite being far more deeply integrated into global value chains than Pakistan.

Beyond labour: environment and the wider picture

Labour is only one part of Pakistan’s broader compliance landscape. The country is also party to 15 major Multilateral Environmental Agreements (MEAs), covering climate change, biodiversity conservation, hazardous chemicals and waste management, ozone layer protection, desertification, and cultural and natural heritage.

The scale of this engagement becomes clearer when viewed over time. The chart below traces the cumulative growth of Pakistan’s international commitments since independence and it shows a country that has, year after year, steadily expanded its participation in international legal frameworks.

Committing to international standards is no simple undertaking. Ratifying a treaty is only the beginning; it requires governments to review their domestic legal framework and, where necessary, amend legislation, strengthen institutions, and align national policies with international obligations.

Pakistan’s 18th Constitutional Amendment, for example, devolved many environmental and labour-related responsibilities to the provinces, creating an extensive compliance architecture that runs from federal ministries down to provincial departments and, ultimately, local governments.

The challenges are real

None of this has been easy, and challenges remain. Even the world’s most advanced economies have yet to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals; Pakistan is no exception.

Part of the reason is that many international standards are negotiated and implemented within sophisticated legal and regulatory systems that are more readily supported by advanced economies. Less developed economies, by contrast, often face additional implementation hurdles owing to resource constraints and competing development priorities.

These challenges are compounded by Pakistan’s geopolitical environment. Sharing borders with India and Afghanistan, the country continues to contend with persistent security concerns and regional instability, adding further pressure on its institutions.

Despite these constraints, Pakistan has repeatedly shown a willingness to update its compliance frameworks in line with emerging global expectations.

International law keeps evolving in response to new global challenges, geopolitical developments, increasingly stringent trade rules, and more complex global value chains.

Most recently, in response to concerns raised by the United States over the risk of forced labour in global supply chains, Pakistan promptly amended its Import Policy Order to prohibit the import of goods produced wholly or partly using forced labour, well before India or Bangladesh adopted comparable measures. As a result, imported products containing inputs produced through forced labour at any stage of the value chain are now barred from entering Pakistan’s market.

The story behind the numbers

The graph above tells only part of the story. Behind every point on it lie years of negotiations, legal reforms, institutional strengthening, and policy decisions. Their impact is rarely visible overnight, but none of that work has gone to waste.

Perhaps it is time to recognise that Pakistan’s engagement with international standards is not a recent phenomenon. It has been quietly laying the foundations for sustainable development for decades.

And this is the Pakistan we must not overlook.

Bangladesh, India scramble to save white-ball series. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is scrambling to save a six-match cricket tour by neighbour India next month, with the foreign ministers of both nations roped in to try to salvage the series.

Comprising three one-day internationals and three T20 matches, the white-ball series was originally planned for August last year but postponed after political relations soured between Dhaka and New Delhi.

“It is being worked on at the ministerial level,” Bangladesh Sports Minister Aminul Haque said late Monday, adding talks were ongoing between the foreign ministers of both nations.

Dhaka and New Delhi have been at odds since Bangladesh’s 2024 mass uprising toppled then-prime minister Sheikh Hasina, who fled to India, her long-time ally, where she remains in hiding.

In February, Bangladesh refused to send a team to India for the T20 World Cup, citing security concerns.

The International Cricket Council (ICC) refused Bangladesh’s request to play their matches in Sri Lanka, and Scotland was drafted in to replace them.

“We want to quickly resolve the deadlock that was created around the Cricket World Cup,” Haque said.

“God willing, we are hopeful that it will be resolved very soon.”

India last toured Bangladesh for a cricket series in 2022 and won a two-Test series 2-0. Bangladesh won the ODIs 2-1.

Bangladesh toured India in September-October 2024 for two Tests and two T20 matches, when India swept both formats.

item.description:
The government’s decision to formulate a five-year strategic plan for reviving Bangladesh’s jute sector is a welcome and timely initiative.
The “golden fibre” remains an important part of the country’s economic heritage, but its potential has long been undermined by outdated technology, weak branding, limited product diversification, and inadequate access to international markets.
To that end, the new Bangladesh Jute Sector Development Strategy and Action Plan 2026-2031 -- which aims to double annual export earnings from around $820 million to $1.64 billion by 2031 -- offers a much-needed roadmap.
However, the real challenge will be ensuring that this plan does not remain another well-intentioned document that gradually loses momentum. Bangladesh has no shortage of strategies and policy announcements; what has often been lacking is sustained implementation, monitoring, and accountability.
The proposed focus on value addition, productivity, competitiveness and export-market diversification is particularly encouraging. Rather than relying predominantly on traditional jute goods, the sector must move towards higher-value products capable of competing in increasingly environmentally conscious global markets.
Investment in research, modern machinery, product design, quality certification, and skilled manpower will be essential to achieving this.
At the same time, farmers must receive better-quality seeds, training, and fair prices so that improvements at the industrial end are supported by a reliable supply of quality raw jute.
Greater coordination between government agencies and the private sector will also be crucial, and recent efforts to strengthen export promotion and market diversification through cooperation between the foreign affairs and textiles ministries are encouraging steps in this direction.
Most importantly, the government must see this plan through to the end. Targets should be accompanied by measurable timelines, regular evaluations, and clear institutional responsibility.
Reviving jute will require patience and consistent investment rather than short-lived enthusiasm.
The sector has immense potential; what it needs now is not another unfinished promise, but sustained commitment to turn this strategy into lasting economic revival.

item.title: Remittance diversification and skills development must go hand in hand. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s record remittance earnings are certainly cause for optimism, but the latest figures also reveal a vulnerability that cannot be overlooked: In FY26, as much as 62% of the country’s remittances came from just five countries.
While this concentration reflects the strength of established migration corridors, it also leaves Bangladesh exposed to economic downturns, labour-market changes, or policy shifts in a handful of destinations.
With remittances reaching a record $35.56 billion in FY26, the time is right to make this vital source of foreign exchange more diversified and sustainable.
Diversifying remittance sources should, therefore, become a deliberate national priority. Bangladesh must actively explore emerging labour markets rather than remaining heavily dependent on traditional destinations.
Diplomatic missions can play a stronger role in identifying opportunities, negotiating labour agreements, and protecting workers’ rights in new markets.
However, entering new countries requires more than simply sending more workers abroad. The global labour market is changing, and demand is increasingly shifting towards skilled workers. Bangladesh must respond by substantially expanding and modernizing skills training.
Technical and vocational education should be aligned with the specific requirements of prospective destination countries, and should also include language proficiency, workplace safety, and knowledge of labour rights.
Most importantly, certification must meet international standards so that Bangladeshi workers are recognized as qualified professionals rather than being confined to low-skilled and low-paying jobs.
A more skilled workforce would open doors to a wider range of countries, and allow individual workers to command better wages. This, in turn, would increase remittance earnings without necessarily requiring a proportional increase in the number of migrants.
The record inflow of remittances demonstrates what Bangladeshi workers can contribute to the economy. The next step must be to broaden where they work and strengthen what they can offer.
Remittance diversification and skills development must go hand in hand if Bangladesh is to build a more resilient migration economy.

item.title: Beyond LDC graduation: Building the next growth model. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The low-cost, labour-intensive strategy that drove much of the country's economic success is reaching its limits in an era defined by artificial intelligence, automation, digital technologies, and intensifying global competition.
Bangladesh now needs a new growth model -- one driven by productivity, technological capability, innovation, skilled human capital, and modern education.
LDC graduation and the transition to upper-middle-income status represent fundamentally different stages of development.
Graduation from the LDC category is assessed on the basis of indicators such as Gross National Income (GNI) per capita, the Human Assets Index (HAI), and the Economic and Environmental Vulnerability Index (EVI).
Moving into the upper-middle-income category, however, requires sustained productivity growth, industrial upgrading, technological innovation, and a highly skilled workforce.
Success will depend not simply on expanding access to education, but on developing the human capital required to power an increasingly knowledge- and technology-driven economy.
The urgency of this transformation is evident in Bangladesh’s workforce. Around 30% have no formal education, while more than 50% have only primary or secondary education. Over 40% remain in agriculture, much of it low-productivity and technologically limited.
Bangladesh's technological landscape reflects a similar reality. While digital connectivity has expanded rapidly, much of the economy still relies on production systems associated with earlier industrial revolutions.
Bridging this gap requires more than importing advanced technologies; it requires developing the human capabilities to adopt, adapt, improve, and ultimately create them.
Bangladesh’s request to the United Nations to extend the LDC graduation preparatory period to November, 2029 therefore presents a valuable opportunity. Rather than viewing the additional time as merely a postponement of difficult decisions, policy-makers should use it to accelerate structural reforms.
The years leading up to 2029 should be a period of purposeful investment in education, industrial upgrading, research, innovation, and workforce development.
Education lies at the heart of this transformation because the nature of work and the skills demanded by the economy are changing rapidly. An education system designed primarily for memorization, routine tasks, and examination performance can no longer adequately prepare young people for a technology-driven and increasingly competitive global economy.
Schools, technical institutions, and universities must therefore prepare learners not only with strong disciplinary knowledge but also with critical thinking, creativity, communication, collaboration, digital competence, adaptability, and a commitment to lifelong learning.
Schools should build strong foundations in literacy, numeracy, ethical values, digital literacy, and problem-solving. At the same time, universities should cultivate research capability, interdisciplinary collaboration, innovation, entrepreneurship, and the ability to generate new knowledge and technologies.
Such a transformation is essential not only to improve the quality of education but also to develop the human capital needed for higher productivity, economic diversification, technological upgrading, and sustainable growth.
Education reform alone, however, will not be sufficient. Bangladesh must simultaneously accelerate industrial transformation through strategic investments in advanced manufacturing, electronics, pharmaceuticals, renewable energy, artificial intelligence, agri-tech, digital services, and high-value engineering industries.
Equally important is stronger collaboration among universities, industry, and government to promote research, technology transfer, innovation, and entrepreneurship.
Unfortunately, much of Bangladesh's education system still reflects the needs of an earlier industrial era. Teaching remains largely lecture-based and students are rewarded more for recalling information than for questioning, analyzing, solving real-world problems, or generating innovative ideas.
Curriculum reform has often followed a predictable pattern: Whenever new knowledge becomes important, another course is added.
Yet every learner has cognitive limits, and overcrowded curricula encourage memorization rather than understanding.
Instead of continually expanding content, Bangladesh should redesign curricula, teaching, learning, and assessment around the competencies increasingly demanded by modern economies.
Active learning, project-based learning, interdisciplinary problem-solving, design thinking, and authentic assessment can better prepare students for a rapidly changing world.
The coming years present Bangladesh with a unique opportunity to align education reform with economic transformation.
A coherent national strategy should focus on five priorities:
Achieving these priorities demands a shared national vision, sustained political commitment, and effective implementation. Bangladesh should establish a high-level national implementation and monitoring mechanism involving government, industry, academia, and other key stakeholders to coordinate reforms, monitor measurable targets, identify implementation bottlenecks, and ensure that progress remains consistent across political and administrative transitions.
Bangladesh has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to achieve ambitious national goals. LDC graduation is itself evidence of decades of determined progress. The additional preparatory period should therefore be viewed not as extra time to maintain the status quo, but as a strategic opportunity to prepare Bangladesh for the next stage of national development.
If the country uses the years leading to 2029 to modernize education, strengthen research and innovation, upgrade its industries, and develop a highly skilled workforce, it will be well positioned to achieve not only upper-middle-income status but also sustained, inclusive, and knowledge-driven development.
Dr MM Shahidul Hassan is Distinguished Professor, Eastern University and Former Vice-Chancellor, East West University.

item.title: Empowering Bangladesh through gender sensitivity, respect, and equality. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh has made remarkable progress in economic growth, poverty reduction, education, healthcare, and women's participation in the workforce over the past five decades. Yet sustainable development cannot be measured solely through economic indicators, infrastructure projects, or technological achievements. The true strength of a nation lies in how it treats its people, particularly women and girls, who constitute nearly half of the country's population.
Despite considerable progress, Bangladesh continues to face deep rooted challenges arising from gender discrimination, limited awareness of human rights, and conservative social attitudes. Although literacy rates have improved significantly, social literacy regarding equality, dignity, respect, and human rights remains inadequate in many communities.
Many people can read and write, but they have not received sufficient education on gender equality, mutual respect, and the rights of women and girls. Consequently, discriminatory attitudes and practices continue to persist in homes, educational institutions, workplaces, and public spaces.
Gender sensitivity is not merely a social concept. It is a transformative approach that promotes equality, protects human rights, and contributes directly to national development.
A gender sensitive society recognizes that women and men possess equal dignity, equal rights, and equal value. It encourages respect for every individual regardless of gender and creates an environment where all citizens can contribute fully to society.
Traditional norms continue to influence behaviour and decision making. In many households, boys enjoy greater freedom, mobility, and opportunities than girls who are often expected to shoulder household responsibilities from an early age, while boys are encouraged to pursue education, careers, and leadership roles.
Such practices create inequality and limit the potential of millions of women and girls.
Equality cannot be achieved through legislation alone. While Bangladesh has enacted laws to protect women from violence, discrimination, and harassment, legal provisions are often weakened by poor implementation, social resistance, and lack of awareness.
Gender sensitivity addresses the root causes of inequality by changing attitudes and behaviours. It teaches people to respect the rights, aspirations, and contributions of women and girls and challenges stereotypes that portray women as inferior or dependent.
Gender sensitivity is equally essential for protecting human rights. Human rights belong to every individual regardless of gender, religion, ethnicity, or social status. Every woman has the right to education, healthcare, employment, property ownership, participation in decision making, safety, and freedom from violence and discrimination.
However, these rights cannot be fully realized unless society embraces the principle that women and girls deserve equal respect and equal opportunities.
National statistics reveal the urgency of this issue. According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics and the United Nations Population Fund, approximately 76 % of women in Bangladesh have experienced some form of violence from an intimate partner during their lifetime.
Child marriage continues to affect thousands of girls each year despite legal restrictions.
Women remain underrepresented in leadership positions and continue to face barriers in employment, access to resources, and justice systems.
These realities demonstrate that economic growth alone cannot eliminate inequality. Social attitudes must change alongside economic progress.
Education offers the most effective pathway to such change. Gender sensitivity, equality, human rights, and mutual respect should be introduced as mandatory subjects from primary education and integrated throughout the national curriculum.
In fact, this learning process should begin even earlier within the family. Parents are a child's first teachers. Children develop values by observing how adults treat one another.
If boys grow up seeing their mothers, sisters, and female relatives respected and valued, they are more likely to become responsible and respectful citizens.
Likewise, girls who are encouraged and empowered develop confidence and leadership skills.
Making gender sensitivity a compulsory subject in schools would help build a new generation that values equality, inclusion, and human dignity. Textbooks should portray women and men equally in leadership, science, business, governance, and public service. Teachers should receive specialized training to ensure that classrooms promote fairness and inclusion.
International experience supports this approach. Countries such as Sweden, Norway, Finland, and Iceland have successfully incorporated equality and human rights education into their school systems. These countries consistently rank among the world's leaders in gender equality, social trust, quality of life, and human development. Their experience demonstrates that teaching respect and equality from an early age can transform social attitudes and strengthen national development.
The workplace is another critical area where gender sensitivity must be enforced. Every government office, private company, educational institution, factory, and service organization should adopt gender sensitive policies and practices. Women must receive equal opportunities in recruitment, promotion, training, leadership, and remuneration. Workplace harassment, discrimination, and unequal treatment must not be tolerated.
Existing laws should be implemented rigorously to ensure safe and equitable working environments. Where legal provisions are inadequate or ineffective, new legislation should be enacted to strengthen protection mechanisms and ensure accountability.
Gender sensitivity should not remain a policy statement; it must become a legally enforceable principle governing all public and private institutions. Regular monitoring, compliance audits, and mandatory gender awareness training should be introduced across sectors.
The benefits of gender sensitivity extend far beyond women and girls. It creates healthier families, stronger communities, and more productive economies. When women are respected and empowered, family incomes increase, children's education improves, healthcare outcomes become better, and communities become more resilient. Men also benefit through healthier relationships, reduced social tensions, and shared family responsibilities.
Gender sensitivity also contributes directly to Bangladesh's commitment to achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Most notably, it advances SDG 5 on gender equality, particularly Target 5.1, which aims to end all forms of discrimination against women and girls, Target 5.2, which seeks to eliminate violence against women and girls, and Target 5.5, which promotes women's full participation and leadership.
The economic implications are equally significant. The World Bank has repeatedly emphasized that countries achieve stronger and more sustainable economic growth when women participate equally in education, employment, entrepreneurship, and leadership.
Bangladesh has already witnessed the transformative impact of women's participation in the ready made garment industry, agriculture, healthcare, education, and public administration. Greater gender sensitivity would unlock even more human potential and accelerate national development.
The media, civil society organizations, religious leaders, policy-makers, and educational institutions all have critical roles to play in promoting positive social attitudes. Public awareness campaigns should challenge harmful stereotypes and highlight the achievements and contributions of women. Gender sensitivity should become a national value reflected in governance, policymaking, public discourse, and everyday behaviour.
Economic progress has created new opportunities, but long term prosperity requires social transformation as well. A nation cannot reach its full potential while half of its population continues to face discrimination, exclusion, and violence.
Shahiduzzaman is the Editor and CEO of News Network.
